content: White sponge nevus, also referred to as Cannon's disease or hereditary leukokeratosis of mucosa, is a genetic condition that follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. While it is typically congenital, meaning present at birth, it can also manifest during childhood or adolescence. The condition arises due to mutations in the keratin 4 (KRT4) and keratin 13 (KRT13) genes. These mutations disrupt the normal function of keratin proteins, which are essential for maintaining the structural integrity of epithelial tissues. Clinically, white sponge nevus is most commonly observed in the oral cavity. It typically presents as thick, bilateral white plaques with a spongy texture. These lesions are most frequently found on the buccal mucosa (the inner lining of the cheeks) but can also appear on the labial mucosa (inner lining of the lips), alveolar ridge (the bony ridge containing the tooth sockets), or the floor of the mouth. Notably, the gingival margin (gum line) and the dorsum of the tongue (top surface of the tongue) are almost never affected. Although the condition is entirely benign and does not pose any serious health risks, it is often misdiagnosed as leukoplakia, a potentially precancerous condition. There is no specific treatment for white sponge nevus, but since it does not lead to significant clinical complications, the prognosis is excellent.
